steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a variational framework for Gaussian process motion planning. It should explain what motion planning involves, review the main kinds of planners and how probabilistic representations are used for uncertainty in nearby areas, and then state what our framework contributes.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What motion planning is and why it is hard
  - robot finds path of motion from start to goal state
  - requirements: collision-free, joint/torque limits, desired end-effector orientation, task-specific requirements
  - smooth, no abrupt/sharp motions
  - high-dimensional configuration spaces; uncertainty (sensor noise, external disturbances, other effects); complex environment dynamics
- Main families of planners
  - sampling-based, e.g. rapidly-exploring random trees: explore trajectory space via stochastic processes (space-filling trees)
  - optimization-based: constrained optimization problem on space of paths
  - probabilistic-inference-based: motion planning as Bayesian inference over paths, solved with inference algorithms
- Probabilistic representations of uncertainty in related areas
  - executing the path on the physical robot
  - probabilistic representations increasingly prominent, e.g. imitation learning
  - probabilistic motion primitives: Gaussian trajectory distributions, learn from expert demonstrations, blending trajectories
  - extension with mixture model: distinct candidate trajectories, uncertainty around each
  - energy-based models + expert demonstrations -> stochastic motion planning primitives
- This work: the vGPMP framework and the link to optimization-based planners
  - probabilistic-inference-based motion planning with Gaussian processes
  - (i) unifying variational Gaussian process motion planning (vGPMP): motion planning as variational inference (optimization over probability distributions)
  - parameterized by waypoints (where plans go through on average), optimized per task
  - (ii) GP motion planners = stochastic extensions of optimization-based planners
  - same capabilities + uncertainty estimates, propagated downstream
- What the framework enables
  - hard and soft constraints (joint limits, collision) in objective; task-independent properties like smoothness
  - interval-based and Monte-Carlo-sampling-based uncertainty quantification, both scalable
  - augments and simplifies earlier GP-based planners; straightforward to implement

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Motion planning is the process of a robot finding a path of motion from a start state to a goal state. The path has to be collision-free, and it has to satisfy constraints like joint limits or torque limits, keep a desired end-effector orientation, and also fulfill other requirements that depend on the task. It should be smooth too, without abrupt or sharp motions. To compute such a path, an algorithm has to deal with robot configuration spaces that can be high-dimensional. There can be uncertainty as well, because of sensor noise, external disturbances and other effects. And the algorithm also has to cope with complex dynamics of the environment.

Modern motion planning algorithms use different mathematical principles to handle these challenges. Sampling-based planners, for example rapidly-exploring random trees, explore the space of possible trajectories using stochastic processes such as space-filling trees. Optimization-based planners get a motion plan by solving a constrained optimization problem on the space of possible paths. Probabilistic-inference-based planners treat motion planning as a Bayesian inference problem over spaces of paths, so motion plans can be computed with inference algorithms.

- Probabilistic representations of uncertainty in related areas
  - path must be executed on the physical robot
  - probabilistic representations increasingly prominent, e.g. imitation learning
  - probabilistic motion primitives: Gaussian trajectory distributions, learn from expert demonstrations, blending trajectories
  - extension with mixture model for distinct candidate trajectories, uncertainty around each
  - energy-based models + expert demonstrations -> stochastic motion planning primitives
- This work
  - (i) vGPMP: motion planning as variational inference, parameterized by waypoints that can be optimized
  - (ii) GP motion planners as stochastic extensions of optimization-based planners; same capabilities plus uncertainty estimates
- What the framework enables
  - hard and soft constraints, smoothness
  - interval-based and Monte-Carlo uncertainty quantification, scalable
  - augments and simplifies earlier GP-based planners

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Motion planning is the process of a robot finding a path of motion from a start state to a goal state. The path has to be collision-free, and it has to satisfy constraints like joint limits or torque limits, keep a desired end-effector orientation, and also fulfill other requirements that depend on the task. It should be smooth too, without abrupt or sharp motions. To compute such a path, an algorithm has to deal with robot configuration spaces that can be high-dimensional. There can be uncertainty as well, because of sensor noise, external disturbances and other effects. And the algorithm also has to cope with complex dynamics of the environment.

Modern motion planning algorithms use different mathematical principles to handle these challenges. Sampling-based planners, for example rapidly-exploring random trees, explore the space of possible trajectories using stochastic processes such as space-filling trees. Optimization-based planners get a motion plan by solving a constrained optimization problem on the space of possible paths. Probabilistic-inference-based planners treat motion planning as a Bayesian inference problem over spaces of paths, so motion plans can be computed with inference algorithms.

After a path is computed, it still has to be executed successfully on the physical robot. Probabilistic representations for handling uncertainty are becoming more and more prominent in a number of related areas, like imitation learning. For instance, probabilistic motion primitives parameterize Gaussian trajectory distributions to learn from expert demonstrations, and they also provide related functionality like blending trajectories together. Another work extends this by adding a mixture model so that distinct candidate trajectories can be handled, with uncertainty around each one. A further work uses energy-based models to integrate expert demonstrations and create stochastic motion planning primitives. These developments show that probabilistic representations are useful for addressing uncertainty in related robotics problems.

In this work we study motion planning based on probabilistic inference with Gaussian processes. First (i), we introduce a unifying variational Gaussian process motion planning (vGPMP) framework. It represents the motion planning problem as a variational inference problem, which is an optimization problem on a suitable space of probability distributions. The problem is parameterized by a set of waypoints. The waypoints describe locations that the motion plans should go through on average, and they can be optimized to find motion plans for a given task. Second (ii), we use this variational inference viewpoint to show that Gaussian process motion planners are stochastic extensions of optimization-based planners. So Gaussian process motion planners implemented this way have the same capabilities as optimization-based planners, and in addition they give uncertainty estimates because of their stochastic construction, which can be propagated downstream.

With our framework, hard and soft constraints such as joint limits and collision constraints can be put directly into the motion planning objective, and also task-independent properties like smoothness. Uncertainty can be quantified based on intervals and also based on Monte Carlo sampling, and both ways are scalable. The framework augments and simplifies earlier Gaussian-process-based motion planners, and it gives practitioners a straightforward way to implement and construct motion plans with uncertainty.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Motion planning refers to the process by which a robot finds a path of motion from a start to a goal state. This path should be collision-free, satisfy constraints such as joint or torque limits, maintain a desired end-effector orientation, and fulfill other task-specific requirements. It should also be smooth, avoiding abrupt or sharp motions. To compute the path, an algorithm needs to handle potentially high-dimensional robot configuration spaces, which may involve uncertainty due to inherent sensor noise, external disturbances, and other effects. The algorithm also needs to cope with complex environment dynamics.

Modern motion planning algorithms handle these challenges using different mathematical principles. Sampling-based planners, such as rapidly-exploring random trees [1,2,3,4], explore the space of possible trajectories via stochastic processes, such as space-filling trees. Optimization-based planners [5,6,7,8,9,10,11] calculate a motion plan by solving a constrained optimization problem defined on the space of possible paths. Probabilistic-inference-based planners [12,13,14,15,16,17] reinterpret motion planning as a Bayesian inference problem over spaces of paths, so that motion plans can be computed using inference algorithms.

Once a path is computed, one must ensure it can be executed successfully on the physical robot. Using probabilistic representations to handle uncertainty is becoming increasingly prominent in a number of related areas, such as imitation learning. For instance, probabilistic motion primitives [18] parameterize Gaussian trajectory distributions to learn from expert demonstrations, and provide related functionality such as blending trajectories together. [19] extend this with a mixture model to handle distinct candidate trajectories, with uncertainty around each one. [20] integrate expert demonstrations using energy-based-models to create stochastic motion planning primitives. These developments highlight how useful probabilistic representations are for addressing uncertainty in related robotics problems.

In this work, we study probabilistic-inference-based motion planning using Gaussian processes. We (i) introduce a unifying variational Gaussian process motion planning (vGPMP) framework, which represents the motion planning problem as a variational inference problem, that is, an optimization problem on a suitable space of probability distributions. This problem is parameterized by a set of waypoints, which describe locations the motion plans should go through on average; these waypoints can be optimized to find motion plans for a given task. We also (ii) show, using this variational-inference-based viewpoint, that Gaussian process motion planners are stochastic extensions of optimization-based planners. As a result, Gaussian process motion planners implemented in this manner share the same capabilities as optimization-based planners, and additionally provide uncertainty estimates due to their stochastic construction, which can be propagated downstream.

Our framework makes it possible to directly incorporate both hard and soft constraints, including joint limits and collision constraints, into the motion planning objective, as well as task-independent properties such as smoothness. We enable both interval-based and Monte-Carlo-sampling-based quantification of uncertainty, each in a scalable way. The resulting framework augments and simplifies preceding Gaussian-process-based motion planners [12,21], giving practitioners a straightforward way to construct motion plans with uncertainty.
